cfg: A 0 to 100 mood score for the crypto market published daily by alternative.me. It mixes price volatility, momentum and trading volume, social media, Bitcoin dominance and Google searches. Low numbers mean people are scared; high numbers mean they are excited. Some traders read extreme fear as a sign that prices are low and extreme greed as a sign of froth, but it does not predict prices.
sfg: MES Stock Fear & Greed (our own composite)

Our own 0 to 100 mood score for the US stock market, made only from free public data so you can check it. It is not CNN’s Fear & Greed Index (that one is proprietary). How it is worked out: Three parts, equal weight. Each is ranked against its own last 252 trading days (about a year): 0 = the most fearful reading of the year, 100 = the most greedy. (1) Market momentum: the S&P 500 compared with its 125-day average. (2) Volatility: the VIX (lower VIX = more greed, so its rank is flipped). (3) Junk-bond demand: the ICE BofA US High Yield spread over Treasuries (a narrower spread = more greed, flipped too). Data: FRED (S&P Dow Jones Indices, Cboe, ICE).
fgscale: 0-24 extreme fear, 25-44 fear, 45-55 neutral, 56-75 greed, 76-100 extreme greed. It describes the mood right now, not what happens next.
vix: The Cboe Volatility Index, often called the market’s “fear gauge”. It is worked out from S&P 500 option prices and shows how much movement traders expect over the next 30 days, as an annual percentage. Around 12-15 is calm, 20+ is nervous, 30+ is fearful, and 40+ usually only happens in a crash or crisis.
momentum: Compares the S&P 500 today with its average closing price over the last 125 trading days (about six months). Well above the average = prices have been rising strongly (greed); below it = falling (fear).
junk: How much more interest risky companies have to pay than the US government, in percentage points. When investors are relaxed they accept a small extra (a narrow spread); when they are scared they demand much more (a wide spread). Series: ICE BofA US High Yield Index option-adjusted spread.
mcap: Price times the number of coins (or shares) in existence. The total crypto market cap adds this up for every coin CoinGecko tracks.
dominance: Bitcoin’s share of the total crypto market cap. Rising dominance usually means money is moving into Bitcoin from smaller coins (often in nervous times); falling dominance means other coins are gaining faster (sometimes called “alt season”).
stablecoin: Tokens designed to stay worth one US dollar (or another currency), such as USDT and USDC, backed by cash, bonds or other assets. Their total supply is a rough measure of how much dollar money is sitting inside crypto, ready to be used.
mood: One line per area of the markets, worked out from this page’s own numbers with fixed rules (listed under the table): fear and greed readings for crypto and stocks, the recent price trend for coins, gold, oil and the dollar, the direction of the Fed, the shape of the yield curve, inflation, the recession odds markets give, and how tense the world is. Red = stressed or falling, green = calm or rising, grey = neutral. It describes now; it is not a forecast. Click a row to see the details on its tab.
funding: On perpetual futures (perps) the two sides pay each other every hour so the perp price stays near the real price. Positive funding = traders betting on a rise (longs) pay those betting on a fall (shorts). On Hyperliquid the normal level is 0.00125% an hour (about 11% a year, paid by longs); well above that means many people are leaning the same way with borrowed money, negative means shorts are the crowded side. Crowded positioning can unwind sharply in either direction; it is not a price forecast.
oi: The total value of perp positions still open (counted once, not long plus short). Rising open interest with rising prices means new leveraged money is coming in; a sudden drop means positions were closed or liquidated.
halving: Every 210,000 blocks (about every four years) the number of new bitcoins paid to miners for each block is cut in half. The 2024 halving cut it from 6.25 to 3.125 BTC. The countdown uses the current block height and the recent average time between blocks, so the date drifts a little.
spark: A tiny chart without axes that shows the shape of the price over the last 7 days (crypto) or 3 months (markets). Green if it ended higher than it started, red if lower.
sp500: An index of about 500 of the largest US companies, weighted by size. It is the most common yardstick for “the stock market”.
nasdaq: Every stock listed on the Nasdaq exchange, heavy in technology companies.
dow: 30 large US companies, weighted by share price rather than size. The oldest of the three main US indexes.
gold: Price of one troy ounce in US dollars (COMEX gold futures, front month). Often bought as a safe haven when people worry about inflation or crises.
oil: West Texas Intermediate crude oil, US dollars per barrel (NYMEX futures, front month). Oil prices feed into fuel, shipping and inflation.
dxy: The US dollar measured against six major currencies (mostly the euro, then the yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona and Swiss franc). Up = the dollar is getting stronger.
fedfunds: The interest rate US banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed sets a target range (for example 4.25% to 4.50%) and steers the actual rate (the “effective” rate) into it. It ripples out to mortgages, car loans, savings accounts and business borrowing.
treasury: The interest the US government pays to borrow for 2 or 10 years, as set by trading in its bonds. The 2-year mostly tracks where people expect the Fed to put rates; the 10-year also reflects long-run growth and inflation expectations, and it drives mortgage rates.
yieldcurve: A line of interest rates for borrowing over different lengths of time. Normally long-term rates are higher than short-term ones (lenders want more to tie money up longer), so the curve slopes up. The 10-year minus 2-year difference is a simple way to measure the slope.
inversion: When short-term rates are higher than long-term rates (10-year minus 2-year below zero). It has come before every US recession since the 1970s, usually 6 to 24 months earlier, but the timing varies a lot, and as of late 2026 the 2022-2024 inversion (the longest on record) had not been followed by an NBER-dated recession. Treat it as a warning light, not a forecast.
recession: Periods the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) dates as US recessions: a significant fall in economic activity that lasts more than a few months. They are dated after the fact, often a year later.
bps: One basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point: 0.25% = 25 bp. Rate changes are usually quoted this way, so a “25 bp cut” takes 4.50% to 4.25%.
fomc: The Federal Open Market Committee: the 12 people at the Fed who vote on US interest rates (the 7 Board governors, the New York Fed president and 4 of the other 11 regional Fed presidents in rotation). It meets eight times a year; the decision is published at 2:00 pm Eastern on the second day, followed by the Chair’s press conference at 2:30.
dotplot: At four of the eight meetings (marked with a dot here) each FOMC participant marks where they think the fed funds rate should be at the end of this year and the next few years. The chart of those dots shows the committee’s range of views. It is not a promise and often changes.
cpi: The Consumer Price Index tracks the price of a basket of things households buy (food, rent, fuel, clothing, services). Inflation here is the change from the same month a year earlier. The Fed aims for about 2% a year, measured with a related index (PCE).
policyrate: The main interest rate a central bank sets. Bank of Canada: the target for the overnight rate. ECB: the deposit facility rate (what banks earn on money left with the ECB). Bank of England: Bank Rate.
pred: Websites where people trade contracts that pay $1 if something happens and $0 if it does not. The price of a “Yes” share, in cents, is read as the crowd’s chance: 70¢ = about 70%. They react fast to news but they can be wrong, thin markets can be moved by a few traders, and they are not available or legal everywhere.
odds: Polymarket shows the last trade price of “Yes”; for Kalshi we use the middle of the best bid and ask. In a market with several answers (“How many cuts?”) the chances should add up to about 100%. A “ladder” like “Above 3.00%, Above 3.25% ...” shows the chance of each level; the most likely range is the step with the biggest drop between two rungs.
vol: How much money changed hands in that market over the last 24 hours. Bigger volume usually means a price that is harder to push around.
doomsday: A symbol, not a measurement. Since 1947 the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (founded by scientists from the Manhattan Project) has set the hands once a year, usually in late January, to show how close its Science and Security Board judges humanity to be to a man-made global catastrophe: nuclear war first, and since 2007 also climate change, and lately biological threats and AI. Midnight = catastrophe. It is an expert opinion, not a probability, and it is not updated when news breaks between announcements.
geoodds: The price of a “Yes” share on Polymarket or Kalshi for questions about wars, ceasefires, invasions and blockades, read as the traders’ chance. We only show the markets’ own numbers: no averaging, weighting or MES index on top. Markets about war are often thin and can be moved by a few traders or by rumours, they can be worded in surprising ways (always read the rules on the market page), and they are not open to everyone in every country.
dated: Some questions are split into dates: “Ceasefire continues through October 31 / November 30 / December 31”. Each date is its own yes/no market, shown here earliest first. For “continues through” the chance usually falls the further out you go; for “happens by” it usually rises.
contracts: Kalshi reports how many contracts were traded, not dollars. Each contract pays $1 if the answer is Yes, so the dollars that changed hands are less than the contract count.
warcost: Official figures come from the Pentagon (testimony or briefings to Congress) and are cumulative totals on the day they were given; what they include changes (some leave out the build-up, base repairs, veterans’ care or interest on borrowing). Think-tank estimates such as CSIS work from Congressional Budget Office unit costs. Long-run studies (for example Brown University’s Costs of War project) count far more, so different numbers can all be honest. We list each with its date and source instead of running a live counter.
etf: US exchange-traded funds that hold real bitcoin (BlackRock IBIT, Fidelity FBTC, Grayscale GBTC and others, trading since January 11, 2024). An inflow means investors bought new fund shares, so the funds bought bitcoin; an outflow means shares were cashed in and bitcoin was sold. Totals for all US spot funds, counted in bitcoin by BGeometrics; the dollar figure is that day’s bitcoin amount times the Bitcoin closing price, so it can differ a little from the funds’ own reports. Big flows show what large investors are doing; they follow the price as often as they lead it.
etfheld: Bitcoin held by US spot ETFs

The running total of every day’s net flow since the funds opened: about how many bitcoins all US spot ETFs hold together. It starts at zero on January 11, 2024, so the bitcoin Grayscale already held in its trust before it became an ETF is not counted.
smartdumb: Two 0 to 100 scores for how bullish two groups of stock-futures traders are compared with the last three years. The idea, made popular by SentimenTrader, is that hedgers (“smart money”) tend to buy when prices have fallen and sell into rallies, while small traders (“dumb money”) tend to chase the trend, so the two often point opposite ways at turning points. It describes positioning, not what happens next; there are long stretches where it says little. How it is worked out: Made from the CFTC’s weekly Commitments of Traders report (legacy, futures only) for four US stock-index futures: E-mini S&P 500, Nasdaq-100, Dow and Russell 2000. Smart money = commercial traders (banks, dealers and big institutions that use futures to hedge). Dumb money = non-reportable positions (traders too small to have to report, mostly individuals). For each market we take each group’s net position (long minus short) as a share of open interest and rank it against the last 156 weeks (3 years): 0 = the most bearish that group has been in 3 years, 100 = the most bullish. The four markets are averaged. Positions are as of Tuesday and published the following Friday, so it is always a few days old. Our own composite, not SentimenTrader’s (theirs is proprietary and uses other inputs).
cot: A weekly report by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission listing how many futures contracts each type of trader holds long and short, as of Tuesday, published Friday afternoon. “Commercials” use futures to hedge their business; “non-reportable” positions belong to traders below the reporting size, mostly individuals.
feargauges: Prices that often jump when people get scared: oil (supply worries, especially around the Strait of Hormuz, where about a fifth of the world’s oil passes), gold (a traditional safe haven), the VIX (expected stock-market swings) and the US dollar. They react to many things besides conflict, so a move is a hint, not proof.
